title: Publish to Paprika
overviewMarkdown:
Publishes a finished recipe straight into Paprika Recipe Manager 3, optionally with a generated food-photography image.

Set the **Service Token** setting to the `SERVICE_TOKEN` from the paprika-aware-chef deployment, and the **Service URL** to its base URL.

Runs server-side, so it works from a phone with no local setup.

userSettings.name: serviceUrl
userSettings.label: Service URL
userSettings.description: Base URL of the paprika-aware-chef deployment, with no trailing slash. For example https://paprika-aware-chef.vercel.app

userSettings.name: serviceToken
userSettings.label: Service Token
userSettings.description: The SERVICE_TOKEN value from the deployment's environment.

openaiSpec.name: publish_recipe
openaiSpec.description: Publish a completed recipe to the user's Paprika Recipe Manager, optionally with a generated food-photography image. ONLY call this once the user has explicitly asked for the recipe to be published - 'publish it', 'send it to Paprika', or an equally plain yes. Finishing the recipe is NOT permission to publish it; the user develops recipes in conversation and decides when one is ready. Send the recipe as it stands after every revision agreed in the conversation, not the first draft. Do not print the recipe as markdown in the chat as well - publishing is the delivery.

description.description: One or two factual sentences saying what the dish is and what is in it. No flourish.

servings.description: Free text, e.g. '4' or '6 to 8'. Use the number the user asked for.

cook_time.description: Free text, e.g. '40 minutes'. Paprika computes the total itself, so do not send one.

ingredients.description:
One ingredient per line, newline separated.

GROUP BY COOKING STAGE, in the order the stages happen. Start each group with a heading line ending in a colon ('Sear the chicken:'), then a blank line before the next group. Paprika renders a line ending in a colon as a section heading, so the list reads in cooking order.

When one ingredient is split across stages, list it in each stage at the amount that stage needs, and note the total on its first appearance: '1 tablespoon olive oil, of 2 tablespoons total'. Do NOT also list it as a separate total line - Paprika's grocery list adds the lines up, and a total line plus the per-stage lines would buy twice the oil.

The quantity MUST come first on every ingredient line ('400 grams tonnarelli', never 'tonnarelli, 400 grams') because that is what Paprika's portion scaling reads. NEVER begin a line with a bullet, dash, asterisk or number - it breaks Paprika's parser. Headings are the one exception to quantity-first, and they must end with a colon.

For metric alternatives write the imperial line, then a line containing only the word 'or', then the metric line.

directions.description: Grouped by phase. Put the phase name alone on a line in bold (**Sear the meat**), then the steps as prose paragraphs beneath it. Blank line between paragraphs and before each phase heading. No numbered steps, no bullets. Include exact temperatures, vessel sizes and sensory cues.

notes.description: Chef's tips, substitutions, make-ahead and storage instructions.

nutritional_info.description: Free text. Leave empty unless the user asked for it.

source.description: Where the recipe came from. Use 'Paprika Aware Chef' for recipes you developed.

source_url.description: URL of the original, when adapting a published recipe.

categories.description: Category names, not IDs, e.g. ['Pasta', 'Italian']. The service creates any that do not exist yet.

rating.description: 0 to 5. Leave at 0 for a new recipe the user has not cooked yet.

generate_image.description: Whether to generate a food-photography image. Set this from the user's answer, never assume.

image_prompt.description: How the finished plated dish should look: ingredients visible, plating, natural window light, shallow depth of field, restaurant presentation. Photographic only - never illustrated or stylized.

image_url.description: The URL of the image the user chose from preview_recipe_images. Pass it back exactly as given. When this is set the chosen image is used as-is and generate_image is ignored, so the picture published is the one they actually picked.

openaiSpec.name: preview_recipe_images
openaiSpec.description:
Generate several food-photography options for a recipe and return their URLs, so the user can see them and choose one BEFORE the recipe is published. Call this when the user has asked to publish and said they want a photo.

Describe the FOOD only, in the three fields subject, surface and serving. Every word about photography - camera, lens, light, plate, grain - is supplied by the service and is the same on every recipe, so do not write any of it here.

Write those fields from the recipe you just developed, NOT from the dish's name. A title says 'charred cabbage'; the camera needs to know it is a two-inch wedge rather than half a head. Give real dimensions, how many pieces, how each was cut, and what the cut surface reveals.

State what things ARE. Never write an exclusion such as 'not bok choy' or 'no sauce' - image models have no negation and weight up whatever you name, so an exclusion summons the thing you meant to avoid. Exclusions are stripped before the prompt is sent.

Takes about 20 seconds, so tell the user the photos are being drawn. Show every returned URL as a numbered markdown image, ask which they want, then call publish_recipe passing their choice as image_url. The links expire after about an hour.

subject.description: THE OBJECT ON THE PLATE, physically. The single most important field. Name the principal component, how many pieces, how it was cut or formed, and its actual size with a real measurement. Then say what the cut or broken surface reveals - layers, grain, crumb, filling. Example: 'One wedge of green cabbage, a triangular slab two inches thick at its wide leafy edge tapering to a point, about five inches long, one of four cut through the core from half a head. The flat cut face shows long pale layers fanning from a firm creamy core strip along the bottom edge.' A reader who has never seen the dish should be able to draw it from this.

surface.description: WHAT THE COOKING DID TO THE SURFACE. Be specific about the evidence the method leaves, because that is what makes a picture read as food rather than as a render. Char is uneven blistering and near-black patches with pale untouched food between, not an even brown coat. A sear is a dry crust. Steaming leaves things moist and slumped. A reduced glaze is glossy and clings; a thin sauce pools flat. Example: 'The cut face is blistered and blackened in uneven patches from a dry cast-iron pan, pale green and untouched between the scorch marks, edges dried and papery.'

serving.description: HOW IT IS SERVED: the vessel, the sauce and where it sits, the garnish and how much. Use the quantities the recipe actually calls for - a teaspoon of sesame seeds is a scatter, not a blanket. Example: 'On a shallow stoneware plate, a thin dark soy-yuzu glaze pooled around the base, a scatter of thinly sliced scallion and toasted sesame.'

count.description: How many options to generate, 1 to 4. Use 4 unless the user asks otherwise: roughly one frame in three still gets the cut or the thickness wrong, so a fourth is what makes it near-certain one of them is right.
